newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FORECAST- Zimbabwe dlr seen eight pct down by 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- Zimbabwe dlr seen eight pct down by 1997.

text.p: The Zimbabwe dollar could depreciate by eight percent against the U.S. dollar by the end of the year but would still be over-valued, market analysts said on Friday.

"At the current rate of depreciation I don't think we will go much beyond 11.0000 against the U.S. dollar. The local unit will probably go down to 11.3000 at the most, a depreciation of eight percent from where it is now," one foreign exchange dealer told Reuters.

He and other analysts believe the Zimbabwe dollar, currently trading around 10.3000 against the key U.S. dollar, is still over-valued, especially in view of annual inflation rate of 17.7 percent in August, the latest figure available.
Officials at the central Reserve Bank were unavailable for comment.
"Most of our companies exporting to (neighbouring) South Africa and Botswana are complaining that their goods are more expensive and that has put them at a disadvantage," one dealer said.

"The dollar should be at 11.0000 now and if it were to hit 11.5000 by December this would be quite a big boost for our exporters...such a depreciation would reduce our disadvantage a bit," said Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of economic and share market analysts Dataworld.
Some foreign currency dealers said the Zimbabwe dollar's fall could be speeded up as annual tobacco sales, a major source of foreign currency for the country, draw to a close later this month.
"With the imminent closure of the tobacco sales I see a possible acceleration in our dollar's fall and that would be good news for our exporters," one dealer said.

But Danny Meyer, president of the Zimbabwe National Chamber of Commerce, argued that the local unit, decontrolled by government in 1991 in line with economic reforms and now directed by forces of demand and supply, had been allowed to fall too much.

"We believe the government has control over macro-economic stability and it should ensure that our currency does not depreciate further. We should be getting some stability in our currency which has weakened considerably over the past four years," Meyer says.
